context.firstUser: A teacher, streamer, coach, or group host who needs to load a named pool, make a random selection, and turn the winner reveal into a shared event.
context.primaryJob: Build and verify a numbered contestant pool, choose a reveal mode, run a fair draw, and clearly celebrate the selected person.
context.desiredResponse: The working surface should feel immediately usable, energetic, fair, and unmistakably NameSnap across phone, tablet, desktop web, and the native iOS icon.
referenceProducts: Wheel of Names — dominant live draw surface and editable pool separation
Picker Wheel — visible pool management, no-repeat state, and presentation-oriented draw controls
Kahoot — high-energy group feedback with strong state changes, without copying its visual identity

blurTest.evidence: At gallery scale, the lavender/black tactile cards, gold winner token, primary violet actions, live stage, red destructive actions, and full-screen celebration remain visually distinct without reading labels.

silhouetteTest.evidence: Desktop and iPad form a producer-console plus live-stage silhouette; mobile forms a stacked setup-to-stage flow; the winner is a full-screen event rather than another generic card.

fiveSecondTest.evidence: The first viewport communicates NameSnap, contestant entry, in-pool count, reveal style, no-repeat state, active pool, and the spin action. The winner viewport communicates the selected name and next actions instantly.

realityTest.evidence: Rendered states use a realistic celebrity roster, numbered eligibility, recent picks, an eight-person destructive consequence, the 16-person free boundary, and a long two-word winner name.

journeyTest.evidence: The same pool count, numbering, eligibility, reveal mode, and recent-winner state persist across setup, full-list sheet, confirmation, upgrade boundary, live stage, and winner celebration.

platformTest.evidence: The 390×844 mobile renders use touch-sized controls and contained sheets; the 1024×1366 iPad render preserves the centered side-by-side work surface; the 1440×1000 desktop render keeps the producer controls and stage visible together.

buyerValueTest.evidence: The screen set shows a complete usable random-draw workflow, including pool management, destructive safety, premium gating at the actual limit, a streamable stage, and a highly differentiated winner moment.

implementationTest.evidence: Production code uses shared design tokens, responsive layout rules, real state transitions, 100 celebration combinations, 5.8-second audio continuity, reduced-motion handling, native emoji asset fallbacks, and opaque 1024×1024 App Store icon output.

screenFindings.finding: The producer panel and live draw stage share the first viewport with a clear primary path and no landing-page hero leakage.
The iPad layout keeps the roster centered within its pane and the live stage adjacent, preserving a credible teacher/presenter workflow.
The compact setup panel preserves task hierarchy, touch targets, labels, and the tactile native-derived border/gradient/shadow system.
The full pool remains readable and manageable in a dedicated sheet rather than compressing the working surface.
The confirmation names the destructive action, affected count, irreversible consequence, and safe cancellation path without clipping.
The paywall remains hidden during normal use, appears at the 17th contestant, differentiates lifetime and monthly choices, and scrolls cleanly on phone.
After a rendered-state repair, the hero artwork paints above the winner card while confetti, name, numbered result, and actions stay legible.
The newly generated drummer art fits the reserved hero zone and matches the existing handmade celebration system at phone size.
The native reset confirmation renders the recycle symbol from the bundled asset rather than showing a missing-glyph box.
On the actual iOS home screen, the final icon reads as a contestant list producing a crowned star winner; it contains no number, date cue, or radial wheel.

independentCritic.categoryFluency: PASS — pool, eligibility, no-repeat, recent-winner, reveal-mode, and presentation controls are native to a random-selection product.
independentCritic.originality: PASS — thick ink outlines, layered lavender shadows, warm-gold selections, expressive typography, and handmade celebration art form a distinctive system without tracing a reference product.
independentCritic.marketingFrameLeakage: PASS — the core viewport is a working producer interface; explanatory marketing copy is downstream and does not replace the product surface.
independentCritic.importedCliches: PASS — the web-only wheel is a functional artifact, while the native icon deliberately uses its real list-to-winner interaction instead of borrowing wheel imagery.
independentCritic.adversarialFinding: The first winner render exposed an invisible hero caused by stacking context. The hero was moved out of the background stacking context and re-rendered with both the existing mascot and a new drummer asset before approval.

repairs: Rebuilt the web workspace with the native NameSnap ink, lavender, warm-white, gold, gradient, radius, and hard-shadow tokens.
Expanded the celebration system from five to ten hero artworks and from fifty to one hundred visual combinations.
Made every celebration soundtrack continuous for 5.8 seconds by looping shorter licensed clips and stopping them on dismissal.
Added a full-screen color pulse for the complete celebration interval while respecting reduced-motion preferences.
Moved celebration hero art out of the background stacking context after the first mobile render showed reserved space with no painted image.
Normalized native emoji variation selectors and mapped alert symbols to bundled image assets with an emoji fallback.
Replaced the native radial-wheel icon, then replaced its date-like numeral, with a list-to-crowned-star composition verified at 128 pixels and on the simulator home screen.
verdict: PASS — the rendered web workspace, celebration states, emoji repair, and final native icon meet the quality floor with no known clipping, missing artwork, misleading calendar cue, wheel mismatch, or runtime error.
